overview: Carved shell, handmade pottery, school records and music illuminate daily life in the Virgin Islands. These traces reveal skill and creativity under very different conditions. The islands now called the U.S. Virgin Islands passed from Danish to United States rule in 1917.

periods.title: Indigenous communities and island connections
periods.summary: Pottery and ceremonial objects on St. John show connections with neighbouring Caribbean islands. These approximate dates describe studied deposits, not the beginning or disappearance of all Indigenous people.

periods.title: Danish colonial expansion
periods.summary: Denmark established a Caribbean colony in the late seventeenth century. Its eventual island group comprised St. Thomas, St. John and St. Croix.

periods.title: First British occupation
periods.summary: British forces temporarily occupied the Danish West Indies during the European wars.

periods.title: Danish administration restored
periods.summary: Danish administration resumed between the two British occupations.

periods.title: Second British occupation
periods.summary: A second British occupation interrupted Danish administration until 1815.

periods.title: Restored Danish rule and slavery
periods.summary: Danish rule resumed. Enslaved people continued to resist bondage; emancipation came on July 3, 1848.

periods.title: Freedom and the struggle over labour
periods.summary: Abolition did not end coercive labour arrangements. The 1849 law restricted workers’ choices, and the 1878 Fireburn uprising challenged their conditions.

periods.title: United States naval administration
periods.summary: After the 1917 transfer, the U.S. Navy administered the islands. Public services changed within a system that retained racial inequalities.

periods.title: Civilian administration and changing institutions
periods.summary: Federal oversight passed to the Interior Department in 1931. Organic Acts in 1936 and 1954 reorganised territorial government.

periods.title: Elected territorial government
periods.summary: Islanders elected their governor and lieutenant governor in 1970. The islands remain a U.S. territory.

items.text: Excavations at Cinnamon Bay on St. John recovered carved shell, stone beads and a small gold-and-copper pendant from layers probably dating to about 1100 to 1200 CE. Kenneth Wild interprets the objects and their placement as evidence of ceremonial offerings. Similar designs elsewhere in the Caribbean suggest connections between communities; matching decoration alone does not prove that one island ruled another.

At the Danish West India and Guinea Company Warehouse in Christiansted, the Slave Wrecks Project uncovered traces of homes occupied by enslaved people during the 1700s and early 1800s. Finds included locally made pottery known as Afro-Crucian ware. These objects preserve the work of enslaved African craftspeople alongside the imposing buildings of the trading company.

Christiansted’s historic buildings combined yellow Danish bricks, local stone and coral blocks. The bricks crossed the Atlantic as ships’ ballast, heavy material that helped balance a vessel. Once unloaded, they became building supplies. A brick could have a sea voyage before settling into a wall.

sections.title: Food, families and going to school

items.text: On St. John, enslavers expected enslaved people to grow their own food on poor plots called provisioning grounds. Cultivation and exchange helped people develop skills and social networks despite coercion. After emancipation in 1848, islanders drew on those connections in activities such as charcoal and bay-rum-oil production. This account concerns St. John, where conditions differed from other islands.

St. John’s 1849 school rules put children aged five to nine in class from eight to eleven on weekdays. Older children, aged nine to twelve, attended Sunday school. Parents or employers could be fined for preventing attendance. Estate labour shaped these arrangements: a place in school did not mean a childhood free of work.

Annaberg’s school building was completed in 1847, but a finished classroom did not guarantee money to run it. A mission report dated August 12, 1856 recorded seventy-five children attending the previously unused building. The records reveal the gap between building a school and staffing it. Knight’s article gives differing opening dates, so the dated report is the firmer reference here.

The Steeple Building in Christiansted became a military hospital under U.S. naval administration. Renovations between 1917 and 1925 added a cistern and toilets. A cistern stores water, a practical concern on islands facing dry seasons. Historic architecture includes the plumbing: a handsome building still needs somewhere for water to go.

A 1919 naval report described expanded preventive care, maternity services, infant welfare and training for local nurses. Access was unequal. Sick members of the Black Virgin Islands Navy Band were sent to the municipal hospital in Frederiksted, rather than the military ward in Christiansted. New services and racial discrimination existed at the same time.

Growing up on St. Croix, Stanley Jacobs and his brothers made banjos from sardine cans because their family could not afford instruments. A sardine can could have a second career in music. Jacobs later became a leading player of quelbe, a Virgin Islands tradition whose songs can combine humour with sharp observations about local life.

Jacobs also worked in elder care, organising social gatherings around music familiar to the residents. A coworker, Stanford Simmonds, taught him melodies and how to make flutes from metal tubing and bamboo. Familiar tunes brought residents together, while practical skills passed from one musician to another.

After emancipation, an 1849 labour law fixed wages and allowed estate workers to change employers only once a year. On October 1, 1878, unrest in Frederiksted developed into the Fireburn uprising. Women remembered as Queen Mary, Queen Agnes and Queen Mathilda were among its leaders. Their titles honour labour resistance, not hereditary monarchies. Freedom from slavery had not brought fair working conditions.

Denmark transferred the islands to the United States in 1917, but citizenship was a separate change: U.S. citizenship was granted in 1927. A change of flag and a change in citizenship were different milestones, a decade apart.

ending.text: Danish rule ended with the 1917 transfer to the United States. The islands continue as a U.S. territory, with living communities and traditions. The map’s 1878 starting point is a snapshot boundary, not the beginning of U.S. rule.
